Chapter 6. Breaking the Habit: Stepping Out of Old Patterns
There’s a strange comfort in our routines, isn’t there? Even when those routines leave us feeling stuck or even a little hurt. Maybe you’ve noticed how easy it is to fall into the same reactions—like snapping at someone you care about, hiding away when you’re afraid, or chasing after approval, even if it leaves you feeling empty.
Think about it like this: old habits are like a pair of shoes you’ve worn for years. Sure, they might pinch or rub in all the wrong places, but they’re familiar. And sometimes, that’s enough to keep us slipping them on, day after day—even when they’re hurting us.
Picture someone who just can’t say no, even when they’re running on fumes. Every time a request comes in, there’s that knot in their stomach, but the word “no” never quite escapes. At the end of yet another long day, they drop onto the couch, feeling frustrated and resentful. And tomorrow? The cycle starts again. But one quiet evening, they finally notice what’s happening. Maybe they remember how, as a kid, saying no meant letting someone down or facing anger. Suddenly, this old habit makes sense—it wasn’t just about pleasing others, it was about staying safe.
Most of us have no idea just how much our lives are shaped by these old strategies. The mind loves what’s familiar, clinging to it even after it’s stopped helping us. But the moment you see a pattern clearly, something changes. The grip loosens, just a little. And here’s something important—this isn’t about blaming yourself for old habits. It’s about noticing them with kindness.
Imagine a friend who’s always their own harshest critic. After a small mistake, those same old words echo in their mind. This time, instead of spiraling into shame, they pause and ask themselves, “Where did this voice come from?” Maybe the answer isn’t obvious. But just asking the question opens up a new path. What if there’s a different way to respond?
Breaking free from these old patterns doesn’t happen overnight. It’s a practice—one where you keep noticing, again and again, those moments when habit tries to take the wheel. Each time you catch yourself—whether you’re about to snap, withdraw, or say yes when you mean no—you get a choice. With practice, the space between your impulse and your action gets wider. And right there, in that space, freedom starts to grow.
Take a manager who’s always felt the need to control every detail. When something goes off-script, anxiety kicks in and the urge to micromanage is almost automatic. But this time, they pause. They take a breath, and let the team figure things out. The result isn’t perfect, but something shifts. Trust begins to build—in the team, and in themselves.
So, here’s the real heart of it: breaking the habit isn’t about getting it “right” every time. It’s about becoming more awake to the ways we box ourselves in, and gently choosing something different. Over time, those old shoes just don’t fit like they used to. The path ahead might feel unfamiliar, maybe even a little scary—but it’s also full of new possibilities.
